19714-with-frederick-the-great-a-story-o:
G. A. Henty wrote adventure novels that taught boys history through war. With Frederick the Great tells the Seven Years' War. Henty opens by weighing the war's stakes. Had Prussia been crushed, he argues, Protestantism might have vanished from Germany. The whole course of later events would have changed. He adds that the war mattered nearly as much to Britain.

Henty's formula put a young hero beside great events. Readers learned campaigns while following invented lives. Frederick's Prussia, fighting larger coalitions, suited that formula well. Henty wrote dozens of such novels, all confident and brisk. This one shows his method at its clearest. History first, adventure as the delivery truck.
20173-the-romance-of-golden-star:
George Griffith wrote The Romance of Golden Star, a tale of lost Inca treasure. A sleeper who looks like an Inca lord draws the heroes' awe. If he woke, he could tell how that lost wonderland truly was. He could answer riddles, disprove lies, and reveal hidden treasure at once.

Griffith wrote bold tales of empire, war, and hidden gold for eager readers. Peru's past gives this romance its temples, tombs, and perilous quests. Greed and wonder pull the party deep into old Inca lands. Readers get lost-world adventure in the rich, pulpy style of its day.
20207-under-wellington-s-command-a-tale-:
G. A. Henty wrote Under Wellington's Command, a tale of the Peninsular War. Henty admits one book cannot hold that whole war in outline. To try would make a history, not a tale, he tells readers. His earlier tale had closed with the passage of the Douro.

That crossing drove the French from Portugal in a bold stroke. Now the tale takes up the thread where it left off. Young heroes serve under Wellington through sieges and hard marches in Spain. Readers get Henty's usual mix of true campaigns and boys' bravery.
20354-jack-of-both-sides-the-story-of-a-:
Jack of Both Sides tells the story of a school war at Brincliffe. New boys were lawful game at many schools of the era. But these new boys were also day-pupils, a great grievance there. Only last term had the first day-boy been admitted at all.

Wiseacres prophesied that Jim Bacon was the thin end of the wedge. Boarders and day boys line up as two camps in the war. School stories turn such splits into battles of honor and wit. Readers get a lively tale of loyalty, prejudice, and boyish combat.
20404-all-round-the-year:
E. Nesbit, best known for her children's novels, also wrote verse, and All Round the Year moves through the seasons in poems. The poems mark the turning months with flowers, weather, and city streets. Many were written with young readers in mind.

One poem follows a busy, dusty wind along cruel streets. The wind reaches the heart of violets and robs them of their sweets. Nesbit then turns the image on people: cold kindness met in the street can blight a poor heart the same way. The book mixes charm with such sharp little truths.
20724-the-man-with-the-broken-ear:
Edmond About, a French writer famed for wit, wrote the fantastic novel sold in English as The Man with the Broken Ear. The letters in the text speak to Leon, far from home, and hint at illness and longing at home. A strange find soon turns that homesick talk into a much odder tale.

About mixes science talk, satire, and adventure in one fast story. The broken ear of the title points to a dried human relic with a past of its own. Readers who like early science fiction with a sharp comic edge will find a brief, strange, and lively book here.
20729-at-the-point-of-the-bayonet-a-tale:
G. A. Henty wrote boys' adventure tales set inside real wars, and his Mahratta War story is a clear case. The text calls the fall of the Mahratta power one of the most stirring pages in Britain's Indian campaigns. Those campaigns ran from Clive's day to a firm British rule across the peninsula.

A young hero moves through marches, sieges, and fights as great powers clash around him. Henty packs in period detail about camps, arms, and Indian courts. Modern readers can see both the pull of the adventure form and the imperial views of Henty's age, held side by side on the page.
20849-the-big-brother-a-story-of-indian-:
Summer 1813 opens The Big Brother, George Cary Eggleston's tale of Indian war. Creek bands in Alabama and Mississippi had turned hostile that year. Quiet days of peace, Eggleston warns, make such times hard for later minds to grasp.

A big brother's care for the young gives the tale its name and heart. Frontier homes, alarms, and fights test that bond to the edge. Eggleston knew war at first hand from his own service. His tale mixes boyhood adventure with a veteran's sense of what frontier fear truly felt like, day by day.
21046-story-hour-readings-seventh-year:
Each great race keeps a heritage of story and song, E. C. Hartwell tells seventh-year readers. Hero songs, origin tales, moral fables, and pure fancy all share that store. Story Hour Readings gathers such goods for the seventh school year.

Hartwell chose tales to hold pupils in the last grammar years with worthy matter. Myths, ballads, history tales, and nature pieces fill the reader in turns. Notes help teachers draw out each tale's point in class talk. The book shows how schools once fed young minds on the world's old stories, held to be a birthright of every child.
21136-for-fortune-and-glory-a-story-of-t:
Lewis Hough opens at Harton, a boarding school much like Eton, before sending his heroes to the Soudan War. A former employee, an Egyptian, has stolen a will from a Dublin solicitor, along with an earlier version of it. Because of that theft, a family lost its money when an Eastern bank failed before the war.

Two story lines run side by side: the hunt for the stolen wills and the fighting in the Soudan. School slang and cricket give the early chapters their flavour. In the end the wills are tracked down and justice is done for the estate, while the war scenes carry their own weight.
21201-journal-of-a-voyage-to-brazil-and-:
Maria Graham sailed to Brazil and lived there through parts of 1821, 1822, and 1823, during Brazil's break from Portugal. Her journal, published in London in 1824, records the voyage and the residence. She admits in her preface that she cut many pages on public and private events before printing.

Graham writes honestly rather than with perfect impartiality, which she calls no virtue in some cases. She gathers facts that reached Europe one by one and records how events felt on the spot. The result is a sharp English traveller's picture of a new empire forming, its court, ports, and daily life.
21242-on-the-irrawaddy-a-story-of-the-fi:
G. A. Henty's preface warns that few of Britain's little wars killed so many, in proportion, as the first expedition to Burma. Stanley, his young hero, sails up the Irrawaddy as war breaks out. Chapter titles carry him from a new career to capture, a ruined temple, and service on the staff.

Burmese general Bandoola, the fight for the great pagoda, and the advance on Donabew all appear. Stanley is carried off and rescued along the way. Henty notes how Burmese forces stripped the country of boats and food, pinning the British in Rangoon through one wet season. Victory humbles Burma's pride by the end.
21326-the-black-bar:
HMS Nautilus patrols the west coast of Africa in George Manville Fenn's tale. She intercepts American and Portuguese slave ships bound to buy human cargoes for the Atlantic crossing. Two midshipmen serve aboard her, and Mark Vandean is the hero. The black bar of the title is a heraldic mark of shame in a family's arms.

Fenn drops Mark into one dreadful situation after another, solved often by something unexpected. The patrol setting shows British sea power used against the slave trade in African waters. Equatorial calms, glistening seas, and sudden action alternate as the Nautilus works her station and Mark's ancestry shadows his name.
21374-tention-a-story-of-boy-life-during:
Private Penton Gray, called Pen, wakes wounded in a ravine after a volley. In George Manville Fenn's Peninsular War tale, the boy bugler Punch lies hurt beside him. British troops are near, but French soldiers hold the ground where the boys lie. They must heal in hiding and then find their regiment.

Helpers along the way include the deposed king of Spain himself. Once back, the commanding officer learns that Pen has the education of an officer. He uses Pen's knowledge of the mountains to lead the troops against the French rear. The attack routs the French, and Private Gray is promoted to officer rank on the strength of it.
21398-black-bruin-the-biography-of-a-bea:
Black Bruin, Clarence Hawkes's 1908 life story of a bear, follows one animal from cubhood in the deep woods. Hawkes wrote many such lives of wild creatures, among them a beaver's tale. Charles Copeland's drawings show the bear's world of forest, stream, and mountain.

The tale opens with theft, a chase, and a wild baby bear learning to live. Bruin meets hunters, traps, and a panther, and learns the ways of his kind. Hawkes tells it as a life, not a pet's romp, with real risk at each turn. Young readers who love true-feeling animal stories will find a full one here.
22100-slavery-and-four-years-of-war:
Joseph Warren Keifer, a Union general and later Speaker of the House, published Slavery and Four Years of War in 1900. His subtitle promises a political history of slavery and a personal history of the war of 1861 to 1865. Keifer opens with slavery's long past, older than written history itself. He traces it from barbaric times into the American republic he helped save.

The second half turns to his own service with Ohio troops. Keifer fought in the Shenandoah Valley and rose to command a corps. His verdicts on generals and campaigns carry a participant's weight. The book joins two subjects that shaped his life: the sin he opposed and the war he fought.
22464-the-last-of-the-chiefs-a-story-of-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Last of the Chiefs, a story of the Great Sioux War. Its young hero, Richard Howard, faces a terrible problem at the start. He feels no fear on his own account, Altsheler writes.

A boy in years, Richard is a man in self-reliance. His boyhood on an Illinois farm taught him wood and field. Where prairies slope up to forest, he learned their ways. He is full of courage, strength, and resource for the trail. The story sets him amid the Sioux wars of the plains. Altsheler's frontier tales were favorites with young readers. This one mixes history, danger, and a capable boy hero.
22537-mr-dooley-in-peace-and-in-war:
Mr. Dooley in Peace and in War, dated 1898, collects Finley Peter Dunne's famous sketches. Mr. Dooley is a Chicago bartender who comments on the news. His pub stands in Archey Road, an Irish-American neighborhood.

There one can see wakes and christenings in American dress. Marriages and funerals of the old country appear modified by usage. The Banshee has been heard many times in Archey Road itself. On All Saints' Eve, pookies play tricks in cabbage gardens there. Dooley's brogue carries sharp satire on politics and war. The Spanish-American War fills many of these pieces with bite. Readers get American humor that presidents themselves read and quoted.
22666-the-rainy-day-railroad-war:
Holman Day wrote The Rainy Day Railroad War, a novel of labor and timber country in Maine. The catalog record gives no year. Day, a Maine journalist and novelist, made his name with stories of lumber camps, ward politics, and the men who ran both.

In the sample, a troubled young man named Parker protests the broken promises made to the work crews. The food was to be free of weevils and spoilage. Instead the Italian laborers went half starved and did poor work, while their padrone pocketed the money meant to feed them. Crooked middlemen, hungry crews, and a railroad pushing through wet country set the conflict. Day writes with a reporter's ear for camps and a reformer's anger at graft.
22755-the-adventures-of-the-little-woman:
The Adventures of the Little Woman, Her Dog and the Pedlar is a children's chapbook in verse, with pictures, of the kind once sold for pennies. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its pages mix a comic rhyme story with short moral poems spelled out in syllables for beginning readers.

In the tale, a dog stops barking and the little woman cries out in comic surprise that now she knows who she is. The companion poem teaches that whatever brawls may disturb the street, peace should reign at home. Birds in their little nests agree, it sings, and it is a shameful sight when children of one family fall out and fight. Such chapbooks were the first books many children ever owned.
22816-the-adventures-of-buster-bear:
Buster Bear wakes up hungry in the Green Forest in Thornton Burgess's 1916 animal story book for children. He yawns on his bed of leaves, watches the first sunbeams chase out the shadows, and shakes himself awake. From that slow morning start, his day of wandering and mischief begins.

Each short chapter puts Buster among his neighbors, the rabbits, squirrels, and other forest folk Burgess made famous. The tales teach natural history through talk and teasing rather than lessons. Buster is strong, a bit greedy, and often outwitted, which keeps him likable. Generations of children met American wildlife through books like this one, and the gentle humor still carries the stories.
23036-dave-darrin-after-the-mine-layers-:
H. Irving Hancock lists the action in Dave Darrin After the Mine Layers. The chapter headings promise a renewed grapple, a mine-sweeper's daily round, and a captain lost overboard. Later comes the hour of despair, a vanishing destroyer, the meeting of searchlights, a cowboy Dane, and a German prisoner who talks at last.

Darrin, Hancock's naval cadet grown officer, fights the Great War at sea in this entry of a long boys' series. Mine warfare made unglamorous, deadly work, and the book sells it as high adventure. The pace is relentless, the patriotism open. Readers meet the war as American boys of 1919 were invited to imagine it, dangerous, technical, and winnable by nerve.
23241-my-daily-meditation-for-the-circli:
J. H. Jowett's My Daily Meditation for the Circling Year, published in 1914, offers a short devotional reading for each day. One entry reflects on Abraham. Abram began his journey, Jowett notes, with no knowledge of where he would end up. He obeyed a noble impulse without seeing what would come of it.

He took one step, without demanding a view of the road ahead. That, for Jowett, is faith: to do what God asks today, and leave the outcome to Him. Readers get brief, plain meditations meant for daily use across a full year.
23263-the-fugitives-the-tyrant-queen-of-:
The Fugitives is a tale of the tyrant queen of Madagascar. Its author warns readers, honestly, that he has shifted time and place a little. He has also mixed his characters and their deeds somewhat, to suit the conditions of his tale and the story he wants to tell.

Even so, he says he strove to avoid exaggeration. His aim was a true picture of affairs at the period treated. The island itself draws his highest praise, as one of the most interesting and progressive in the world. Readers get adventure under a feared queen, with a storyteller who admits where invention begins.
a-short-history-of-the-great-war: A. F. Pollard condenses the Great War into a short, clear history — its causes, campaigns, and consequences. Written while memories were fresh, it served a generation seeking to understand. A solid first account of the catastrophe. Maps, battles, and home-front trials are set forth in admirable brevity.
aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war: Frederick Talbot's 1915 account of military aviation in the First World War, written as the new weapons were proving themselves. He describes reconnaissance planes, bombers, Zeppelin raids, and the brave young pilots who flew them. A contemporary record of warfare's newest dimension, valuable for seeing the air war through the eyes of those who watched it begin.
an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-exposition-ex: Sheldon Cheney guides art lovers through the great San Francisco exposition — its architecture, sculpture, and mural paintings clearly explained. ballads-of-peace-in-war: Michael Earls's Ballads of Peace in War: wartime verse. The Jesuit poet's Great War ballads. Earnest and musical. A soldier-poet's songs, earls's wartime ballads, earnest and musical, a soldier-poet's songs, wartime verse, Michael Earls.
bleek-comparative-grammar:
Wilhelm Bleek published his Comparative Grammar of South African Languages in 1862. The German scholar worked in Cape Town among speakers of many tongues. His book founded the true study of the Bantu language family.

Bleek showed that the Bantu tongues form one great linked family. He worked out their sound laws as Grimm had for Europe's tongues. Noun classes and shared roots lock his case into firm order. The feat ranks among the age's great wins in language science. Scholars still cite his Cape Town work as the field's true start point. Bleek gave African tongues the same respect long given to Europe's.

Egyptian theory, he argues, gave the Ka an existence of its own, immortal and awaiting resurrection. The novel builds royal romance on that ancient belief in the double self.
mr-punch-s-history-of-the-great-war:
Charles Larcom Graves edited this Punch record of the Great War, issued in 1919. Punch was Britain's famed comic magazine. The book went through seven printings in a few months. A verse note thanks the writers and artists who made it.

The prologue recalls Punch watching wars since its early days. It names the Crimea, the Mutiny, and the rise of Prussia. Then it turns to five hard years just ended. Cartoons, jokes, and verse carry the tale of the home front. The mix shows how Britons used humor to bear fear, loss, and hope.
my-second-year-of-the-war:
Frederick Palmer reports his second year at the front in this 1917 book. Dodd, Mead issued it in New York. Palmer had written My Year of the Great War before it. Chapter one takes him back to the front at once.

Verdun and its sequel fill the next long chapter. Then comes the Somme: the blow, its first results, and its guns. Palmer tells of Contalmaison stormed and a brigade that went through. A Canadian innovation earns its own chapter. The book is a skilled American reporter's plain record of the war's hardest year, seen from the lines.
nasa-tm-19660012950-observed-ultraviolet:
Spectrograms of Mars, taken from a sounding rocket, give the measure of how strongly that planet reflects ultraviolet light. On March 19, 1965, an Aerobee rocket rose from White Sands Missile Range carrying the instrument. Its camera was built by the Kollmorgen Corporation, with a special wide-field design. A grating spread the light into a spectrum for study.

Ultraviolet light never reaches the ground, so rockets must carry the camera above the air. How much ultraviolet Mars reflects reveals facts about its thin atmosphere. Comparing the measure with a model atmosphere tests that model. The flight was brief, but the spectrograms preserved data no ground telescope could gather at the time.
nasa-tm-19680017356-review-of-recent-bal:
Thomas N. Canning, Michael E. Tauber, and Max E. Wilkins of Ames Research Center review ballistic range tests on ablating cones in this paper. The question is whether smooth laminar flow can cover much of a blunt cone during very fast entry. Such cones model capsules returning through the atmosphere at extreme speeds.

Models ablating in the range matched mass transfer rates expected in real flights up to high entry speeds. Early data compared total ablated mass with laminar and turbulent predictions. Measured values fell between those two extremes. Triangular wedges of heavier removal marked where turbulent flow began. The review tracks how those patterns grew as test conditions changed.
nasa-tm-19680023899-analysis-of-launch-w:
Larry A. Manning, Byron L. Swenson, and Jerry M. Deerwester, of NASA Headquarters' Mission Analysis Division, wrote this September 1968 memorandum, TM X-1651. They analyze launch windows from circular orbits for representative round-trip missions to Mars. A launch window is the limited span when a ship can leave and still reach Mars with the fuel it carries.

The summary opens by defining representative windows and the velocity changes each one demands. Chapters lay out the method, from orbit geometry and quick thrust burns to costly plane changes. Later sections work a typical case, covering Earth and Mars windows and how sensitive fuel needs are. Appendices treat three-burn trips and departure needs at both planets.
nasa-tm-19690024022-hydromagnetic-observ:
K. W. Ogilvie and L. F. Burlaga of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this July 1969 paper, numbered X-616-69-303, on hydromagnetic observations in the solar wind. Plasma and magnetic data from Explorer 34, carrying a Goddard-University of Maryland experiment, supply the evidence. Hydromagnetics treats the solar wind, the Sun's streaming outflow, as a magnetized fluid with waves and shocks of its own.

At boundary surfaces between wind streams, the field ran parallel to the surface, as tangential discontinuity theory requires. Sharp speed jumps there hinted at gliding motions, with indirect signs of swirling instability. Several traveling shocks obeyed the standard shock relations well. Sudden storm commencements, they find, almost always trace to such shocks, while smaller sudden impulses have mixed causes.
nasa-tm-19690027648-variations-in-electr:
N. C. Maynard and J. P. Heppner of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this August 1969 preprint, X-642-69-374. They report variations in electric fields measured from polar orbiting satellites. New probe techniques, using long antennas on rockets and satellites, had just made such direct field measurements possible. The paper asks what fields exist above the poles, and how they change.

Theory pictured the fields as smooth convection patterns tied to ionospheric currents. Maynard and Heppner note that smooth patterns explain only the gross behavior. Smaller scale irregular structure must be understood to explain auroral shapes and forms. Barium cloud drift studies tracked field changes over time, while the satellite probes map changes over space. Their purpose is defining the fields' true character more closely.
nasa-tm-19700026395-mission-d-as-504-104:
Mission D has its final Apollo abort summary in this Houston internal note, dated January 2, 1969. The mission flew with vehicle AS-504. Mission D was Apollo 9, the first crewed test of the lunar module in Earth orbit, flown on the Saturn 5 rocket.

The document gathers crew procedures into a single reference for training. It covers normal Saturn 5 flight, aborts, and abort entries, with the basic text matching the procedures crews would actually use. A limits table divides the climb into abort modes by time and altitude, from low altitude escape tower modes onward. Later modes run through full lift entry, service module engine returns, and an engine burn all the way to orbit.
nasa-tm-19710003362-magnetic-susceptibil:
D. E. Hegland and D. R. Behrendt of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It measures how strongly several rare earth compounds answer a magnetic field. The compounds join rare earth metals with selenium or tellurium.

The team cooled the samples close to absolute zero and raised the field step by step. Most of the compounds showed signs of antiferromagnetic order, the authors report. In that state, atomic magnets line up in opposed ranks and cancel out. One compound showed its own magnetization at the coldest settings. In most cases the pull per atom matched the value figured for the charged rare earth ion.
nasa-tm-19710004288-a-comparison-of-sphe:
Raymond M. Hicks and William R. Harper Jr. of the Ames Research Center ran this wind tunnel study. It compares two shapes used to trip a boundary layer into turbulence at supersonic speeds. The shapes are small spheres and small triangles on a flat plate.

A trip forces the smooth flow next to a surface to turn rough at a chosen point. The team placed the trips at varied distances from the plate's leading edge. Tests ran in the Ames supersonic tunnel across several Mach numbers. Knowing which shape trips the flow best helps engineers design test models. It also keeps tunnel data honest about real flight.
nasa-tm-19710012088-three-investigations:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this memorandum, NASA TM X-64577, dated February 11, 1971. It gathers three investigations of the interstellar medium, the thin gas spread between the stars. One study concerns how X-rays fade as they cross space. The catalog record also points to the physical state of a hydrogen cloud.

The abstract opens with a clear claim. X-ray weakening in space is concentrated inside clouds of gas. Outside the clouds, the weakening is far smaller. That pattern tells astronomers where the absorbing matter sits. Work like this helped map the structure of gas that stars and planets later form from.
nasa-tm-19710014565-numerical-analysis-o:
Raymond C Clerkin of the Lewis Research Center wrote this April 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2270. It works through the numerical solution of two linked integral equations. One equation is of Volterra type and holds a singularity that needs special care. The other is of Fredholm type and contains a principal value term.

Clerkin explained how to compute the principal value part. He tested the technique on a hard integral whose answer was already known. Reaching a stable repeated solution took two fixes. He lowered the relaxation factor and forced one function to stay smooth near the singularity. Such methods support later computer work on tough math problems.
nasa-tm-19720022951-diminiode-performanc:
Arthur L Smith, Richard B Lancashire, Eugene J Manista, and James F Morris of the Lewis Research Center mapped this tiny power device in September 1972, as NASA TM X-2587. The device is a diminiode, a miniature thermionic diode that turns heat into current. Its emitter was a tantalum alloy called ASTAR-811C. The collector used niobium with one percent zirconium. A guarded collector kept the readings clean at the edges.

A computerized facility swept and recorded the performance map. The gap between the hot emitter and collector stayed fixed. It measured only a quarter of a millimeter across the flat faces. Such small diodes served as test vehicles for bigger converters. Their maps showed how new electrode materials behaved. The work continued a long Lewis program in thermionic power.
national-association-for-the-advancement:
Published in New York in April 1919, Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States counts mob killings from 1889 to 1918. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People issued it from its office at 70 Fifth Avenue. The price on the title page was fifty cents.

Front pages list other pamphlets the group had printed on the same crime. Titles name President Wilson's 1918 statement on mob violence and probes in Georgia counties. Other items cover East St. Louis, Memphis, and Abbeville. Put together, the book gave readers a plain record of lynching and of early work against it.
native-races-and-the-war:
Josephine E. Butler published Native Races and the War in London in 1900, while the South African war was still being fought. She dedicated the book to her children and grandchildren. Her opening chapter asks why yet another book on the South African question was needed.

Butler argues that future peace must rest on justice for coloured men as well as white men. She recounts the Transvaal from 1877, its taking by Britain, and its release in 1881. She prints speeches and protests by native chiefs, and proof about slavery there. Her case rests on hearing the native races themselves.
neutral-rights-and-obligations-in-the-an:
Robert Granville Campbell published this study in 1908, growing out of work in the political science seminary at Johns Hopkins. It forms part of a larger study of the causes of the Anglo-Boer War. Its theme is the law that bound countries not fighting in that war.

Britain first treated the fight as too small to wake the neutrality laws of others. By late November it put the war on a plain footing as a war. It dated the start to the Transvaal ultimatum of October 11, 1899. Campbell asks how far the United States met its neutral duties. He then turns to European governments, and to trade with neutrals in wartime.
new-latin-grammar:
Charles E. Bennett, Goldwin Smith Professor of Latin at Cornell, wrote this New Latin Grammar for students. Copyrights run from 1895 through 1918, and Bennett dated his preface at Ithaca on May 4, 1918. He calls the book a revision of his 1908 grammar, with no deep changes.

Bennett added an opening account of how the Latin language began and grew. He hoped keen pupils would find it useful and pleasing. Small fixes sharpen rules, and syllable division now follows Roman practice, he says. Long vowels are marked in more endings than before. An index at the back points to the sources of examples used in the syntax.
on-war:
Carl von Clausewitz wrote this classic study of warfare. Colonel J. J. Graham translated it into English. The first edition of that translation appeared in 1874. A revised London edition followed in 1909, in three volumes. Colonel F. N. Maude added introduction and notes.

The introduction calls war force used for a political object. It praises Clausewitz's deep, philosophical analysis of war. Events since Waterloo follow his teachings, the editor claims. Napoleon first taught the lessons Clausewitz set in form. No book has shaped military thought more strongly. The notes liken his work to what Darwin did for life science. Two famed battle fields gave that same hard lesson, he adds.
othmar: Othmar is a novel by Ouida, pen name of Maria Louise Ramé. This new edition was printed in London in 1886. The catalog dates the work 1885. our-navy-in-the-war: Lawrence Perry's Our Navy in the War is a wartime account of the United States Navy in the First World War. Scribner's published it in October 1918. peace-theories-and-the-balkan-war:
Norman Angell, author of The Great Illusion, published Peace Theories and the Balkan War in 1912. The Balkan War had just broken out, and critics said events had refuted his famous argument. The book opens by quoting a Sheffield speech of Winston Churchill asking who would still say that force is never a remedy.

Angell answers his critics and tests his theory against the new war. He had argued that conquest no longer pays in a world bound by trade and credit. The pamphlet is a defence written under fire, while the war it discusses was still being fought.
pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens Pellucidar with a prologue told by a big-game hunter. The narrator is packing for northern Africa when a letter postmarked Algiers pulls his departure forward by twelve days. The letter draws him into the story that follows, of the hollow world inside the Earth.

Pellucidar continues the adventures of David Innes, who returns to that inner world to free its human tribes from the reptilian Mahars. The chapter titles promise lost travellers, cave-prisons, raids, and conquest and peace. It is pulp adventure at full stretch, with a stone-age world lit by a central sun.
plays-of-near-far:
Lord Dunsany's Plays of Near and Far was first printed in December 1922 by G. P. Putnam's Sons, in London and New York. The edition was limited to five hundred copies. A front list names his earlier books, from The Gods of Pegana to The Chronicles of Rodriguez.

The contents page opens with The Compromise of the King of the Golden Isles, on page one. The Flight of the Queen follows, a longer play that starts on page twenty-one. A third piece, Cheezo, begins on page sixty-five, as the list shows.

springhaven-a-tale-of-the-great-war: R. D. Blackmore's Springhaven — his last novel — tells of England's great war against Napoleon, with smugglers, sailors, and village folk caught in vast events. the-history-of-the-thirty-years-war: A history of the devastating 1618-1648 conflict that ravaged central Europe, written by Friedrich Schiller, the great German poet and playwright. the-world-war: The World War narrates the huge conflict of 1914 to 1918. Great armies, navies, and nations clash across whole continents. The vast history unfolds in clear and orderly sequence. A full and careful record of the Great War.
two-months-in-the-camp-of-big-bear: Theresa Gowanlock and Theresa Delaney were taken captive during the North-West Rebellion of 1885, when Big Bear's Cree band seized them in the Frog Lake tragedy. un-doc-haile-selassie-s-address-on-inter:
Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia gave this address for International Education Year in 1970. The United Nations had set 1970 aside for schooling, with UNESCO in the lead. Two thirds of the world's people still lacked any real chance to learn. Ethiopia had made study a top claim on its funds.

war-and-the-future-italy-france-and-brit: H. G. Wells's 1917 report from the Western Front and Italy: the great prophet of science fiction turns war correspondent. Tanks, trenches, and his vision of what the war means fill these dispatches. Wells witnessing history as it happened.
why-we-are-at-war: President Woodrow Wilson's historic war message of April 1917 asked Congress to take America into the Great War — to make the world safe for democracy. These pages preserve the speech and its context. A landmark of American oratory and a fateful moment in world history.
with-lee-in-virginia-a-story-of-the-amer: G. A. Henty's 1890 With Lee in Virginia: a boy's adventures with the Confederate army. Henty's best American tale, thrilling and vivid. The Civil War for young readers. A boy rides with Marse Robert, henty's Civil War classic.
young-knights-of-the-empire-their-code-a: Lord Baden-Powell, the founder of Scouting, offers more yarns and teachings for his young knights of the empire.
